body:
We make Kiron, and Kiron imports some of these files, so weigh this accordingly. The steps for each app come from its own help pages and App Store listing, checked November 15, 2026. Where an app doesn't publish a step, we say so and name our source instead. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

Your training log is data you can't recreate: every top set, every rep record, years of showing up. Exporting it is how you keep it when you switch apps, cancel a subscription, or just want to look at it in a spreadsheet. The catch is that every app puts the button somewhere different, and two of the six apps here don't put it in the app at all.

Below are the steps for Fitbod, Strong, Hevy, JEFIT, Boostcamp and StrongLifts, what each file contains, and where it can go next.

Where each app's export lives, as of November 15, 2026
AppWhere the export isWhat you getWatch out for
FitbodIn the app: Settings, Export Workout DataCSV, one row per setCheck the unit in the weight column's header
StrongIn the app: Settings, Export Strong Data (Export Data on Android)CSV, one row per setThe file often doesn't say pounds or kilograms
HevyIn the app: Profile, Settings, Export & Import Data, Export Data, Export WorkoutsCSV, one row per setBody measurements are a separate export
JEFITOn jefit.com: Settings, Data Controls, Export DataOne file with your whole historyNot in the app; the file comes in sections
BoostcampNo documented exportNo fileAsk support for a copy
StrongLiftsIn the app: Settings, Export DataCSV, sent by emailA separate route exists if the paywall blocks you

Before you export: three habits that save trouble

  1. Export before you cancel or delete. JEFIT's FAQ, for one, warns that deleting your account removes your workouts and history for good, and tells you to export first. A subscription change can also get in the way: some StrongLifts users said in 2026 that the paywall kept them from their old data.
  2. Switch the app to English first if you'll import the file somewhere else. Column names follow the app's language, and importers look for the English ones. Hevy's help center asks for Strong files exported in English, and Kiron reads English exports only.
  3. Keep the original file untouched. Save it somewhere safe and work on a copy. Re-saving a CSV in a spreadsheet can reformat dates and separators, and third-party importers warn it can break JEFIT's multi-section file.

Fitbod

  1. Open Fitbod's Settings. Independent guides put it behind the gear icon on the Log tab.
  2. Tap Export Workout Data.
  3. Save the file to Files, or send it to yourself by email.

What's in it: a CSV file, which independent guides call WorkoutExport.csv, with one row per set: the date and time, exercise, reps, weight, duration in seconds, distance in meters, incline, resistance, whether the set was a warm-up, and a note. Nothing in the file names the workout, so anything that imports it has to group sets by time. The weight column puts its unit in the header, such as Weight(kg). Guides disagree on whether that follows your Fitbod unit setting, so check the header before you trust the numbers.

Source note: Fitbod's help center doesn't document its export; we searched it on November 15, 2026. These are the steps Kiron's import screen gives, and two independent guides describe the same path.

Strong

  1. Open Strong's Settings.
  2. Tap Export Strong Data. Strong's help center says the Android app calls it Export Data.
  3. Save or share the file. Strong's App Store listing says the export goes to Notes or email, in CSV format.

What's in it: one row per set, with the date, workout name, duration, exercise name, set order, weight, reps, distance, seconds, notes, workout notes and RPE. The weight column usually doesn't say whether it's pounds or kilograms, so open the file and check a lift you know. One App Store reviewer said in September 2025 that, after an update, their export listed kilograms even though the app was set to pounds.

Strong's help center also says exported files can't be imported back into Strong. It's a one-way door, so keep the file.

Hevy

  1. Open your Profile, then Settings (the gear icon).
  2. Tap Export & Import Data, then Export Data.
  3. Choose Export Workouts. Export Measurements gives you a separate file of body measurements.

What's in it: one row per set, with the workout's title, start and end times, description, exercise, superset, exercise notes, set number and type, weight, reps, distance, duration and RPE. Unlike Strong's file, Hevy's puts the unit in the column name, such as weight_kg or weight_lbs, so there's nothing to guess.

JEFIT

JEFIT's export is on its website, not in the app. Its FAQ gives these steps:

  1. Log in at jefit.com.
  2. Open Settings.
  3. Go to Data Controls and choose Export Data.

You don't need to pay for it. In JEFIT's words, "Your training data is yours to download at any time, in every account."

What's in it: JEFIT's FAQ doesn't describe the file. Third-party importers describe a single CSV file covering your whole account history, split into several sections and named after your username and the export date. They also warn that re-saving it in a spreadsheet can break that structure, so open a copy.

Boostcamp

Boostcamp doesn't document a way to export your history. There's no export in its FAQ, its App Store description or its recent release notes, checked November 15, 2026. Your options:

  • Ask support for a copy. Boostcamp's privacy policy (last updated November 27, 2024) says people in the EU, UK and EEA have a right to data portability, and that people in California and some other US states may have a right to a portable copy of their personal information. Requests go through its support team, via its contact page. Asking for your workout history as a CSV file costs nothing, wherever you live.
  • Copy it by hand. For a short history, typing your main lifts into a spreadsheet is slow but reliable.
  • Be careful with browser extensions. Third-party extensions say they can save your Boostcamp history from its website. They aren't made by Boostcamp and we haven't checked them, so think about what account access you'd be handing over.

StrongLifts

StrongLifts' support page, updated October 17, 2026, gives two routes. The usual one:

  1. Open StrongLifts and go to Settings, then Export Data.
  2. Your data appears as a CSV document.
  3. Tap the Share button to email yourself a copy.

If you're stuck on the paywall: StrongLifts has been subscription-only since 2025, and 4 of its 500 most recent US App Store reviews said that kept them from exporting their old data. The support page now covers that case: tap the menu icon in the top right corner, tap Contact Support, and send the pre-filled email to your own address. Your data arrives in that email as a CSV document.

What's in it: StrongLifts doesn't list the columns. Open it in a spreadsheet to see what came across.

Where each file can go

What can read each export, as of November 15, 2026
Export fromHevyKironA spreadsheet
FitbodNo official importYesYes
StrongYesYesYes
HevyNo: Hevy imports Strong files onlyYesYes
JEFITNo official importNoYes, with some tidying
StrongLiftsNo official importNoYes

Boostcamp isn't in the table because there's no documented file to move. Other apps advertise importers for some of these files too, so check the help pages of whichever app you're moving to.

Into Hevy: Strong files

Hevy officially imports Strong exports. In Hevy, go to Profile, Settings, Export & Import Data, Import Data, Import Strong CSV, then choose the file. Hevy's help center asks for an unedited export from Strong, in English and in kilograms, allows one CSV import at a time, and lets you revert an import from the same screen. Routines don't transfer, since Strong's file holds finished workouts only, and supersets arrive as separate exercises. For history from any other app, Hevy's help center says its support team can send a sample CSV in Strong's format, which you could fill in from your own export.

Into Kiron: Fitbod, Strong and Hevy files

Kiron (that's us) imports Fitbod, Strong and Hevy exports. Go to Settings, tap Import from another app, then Choose file. When you first set up Kiron, the same screen opens from "Bring your workout history". Nothing is saved until you've seen a preview:

  • What's in the file: how many workouts, their date range, and how many working sets, not counting warm-ups. Workouts already in Kiron are skipped, so importing the same file twice doesn't double anything.
  • The unit question: when a file doesn't say whether it's in pounds or kilograms, as Strong's often doesn't, Kiron shows your heaviest set and asks which it is. It asks about miles or kilometers the same way.
  • The match list: how many of your exercises match Kiron's library, grouped into "Not in Kiron's library", "Worth a check" and "Matched". Tap any one to use the suggested match, choose another Kiron exercise, or keep it as your own exercise.
  • Removing it again: the import screen lists what you've brought in from each app, with a button to remove it. Imported workouts come out of your history, progress and records; workouts you logged in Kiron stay, and you can import the same file again later.

It brings in finished workouts only, so routines and programs stay behind, and it needs a connection while it runs.

One more thing before you move your history into Kiron: it has no export of its own in version 1.2. Keep your original file.

Into a spreadsheet: everything

Every file here opens in Google Sheets, Excel or Numbers, which makes a spreadsheet the one destination that takes all of them. A few tips:

  • Use the spreadsheet's import option rather than double-clicking the file, so you can choose the separator and keep dates from being reformatted. If everything lands in one column, the file probably uses semicolons, which some apps write when the comma is the decimal point.
  • With one row per set, as in the Fitbod, Strong and Hevy files, filter the exercise column to see a lift's whole history, or chart the heaviest weight per date.
  • Split JEFIT's sections onto separate sheets before you try to analyze them.

If you're tempted to keep training from the spreadsheet itself, our comparison of workout spreadsheets and apps covers the trade-offs.

If you're switching apps

Exporting is the easy half. The harder question is where to go, and we've written that up app by app: alternatives to Strong, alternatives to Fitbod, what to do now StrongLifts is subscription-only, and Hevy vs Kiron. Each one says who should stay put. For the wider view, our roundup of workout apps for following a program sorts eight apps by the job they do.

And the pitch, once. Kiron is a workout app for {{kiron:cell-platforms}} that runs a plan on a calendar: one of 36 ready-made programs, one its AI builder writes, or one you paste in or photograph, with runs and rides on the same calendar as your lifts. If your history is in Fitbod, Strong or Hevy, it comes along through the preview above. {{kiron:pricing-sentence}} If all you want is a safe home for your history, a spreadsheet does that for free. See what Kiron does.

Common questions

Can you export your data from Fitbod?

Yes. In Fitbod's Settings, tap Export Workout Data and save the CSV file. It has one row per set, and the weight column's header names its unit.

How do I export my Strong data to CSV?

Open Strong's Settings and tap Export Strong Data, or Export Data on Android. Strong can't import that file back, so keep the original.

How do I import my Strong workouts into Hevy?

Export from Strong with the app set to English. Then in Hevy, go to Profile, Settings, Export & Import Data, Import Data, Import Strong CSV, and choose the file. Your finished workouts come across; your routines don't.

Can I export my workout history from Boostcamp?

Not with a documented button, as of November 15, 2026. Ask Boostcamp's support team for a copy through its contact page; its privacy policy describes data portability rights in the EU, UK and EEA, and in some US states.

Do I need JEFIT Elite to export my logs?

No. JEFIT's FAQ says every account can export, on jefit.com: Settings, Data Controls, Export Data.

Can I get my StrongLifts data out without subscribing?

StrongLifts' support page gives a route for anyone stuck on the paywall: tap the menu icon in the top right corner, then Contact Support, and send the pre-filled email to yourself. Your data comes back as a CSV document.
